units.translation: Hermann understood that the words ἴυζε καὶ βόα [cry aloud and shout] are repeated from the preceding lines, and he corrected the rest as follows: χέουσα καὶ πικρότερον οἰζύος νόμον [pouring forth also a strain more bitter than lamentation].
Earth, one form of many names.
From where do you utter the name of my father?
O name of Salamis, most hateful to hear.
Throwing back his eye (thus Schuetz for ὄνομα [name]) he calls upon the might of Polyneices, and twice at the end he utters the name in full.
And Phoebe's name is derived from her.
Tell me now this all-wise name.
Cry aloud and shout, having a name more bitter than griefs of lamentation.
Why must I tell you the name?
What name then will mortals give to them?
pouring forth also a strain more bitter than lamentation
Who ever named her so truly in every way, the spear-won bride, the much-contested Helen?
And the seven daughters of Atlas, named.
The mating of horses and donkeys.
Abominating the marriage with the sons of Aegyptus.
With a newly cut furrow of the nail.
Plutarch Mor. 632 f records from Aeschylus' Cabeiroi the phrase ὄξους σπανίζειν δῶμα ποιήσαντας [having made the house lack vinegar], about which see on fr. 96 and Lobeck Aglaoph. p. 1207.
having made the house lack vinegar
Then you will shell a bittersweet pomegranate.
The scholiast explains it by ὀξύθυμοι [sharp-tempered].
And the sharp-hearted ones divided the possessions.
Thus Pearson for ὀξυμηνίτου [of sharp wrath]. The scholiast reads the accusative, explaining it as φόνους ἐφ᾽ οἷς ταχέως μηνίσουσιν Ἐρινύες [murders at which the Erinyes will quickly be wrathful].
To divide the sharp-wrathful judgments of murder.
murders at which the Erinyes will quickly be wrathful
The scholiast explains it by ὀξυτάτοις θρήνοις [with most piercing laments].
Scholiast: τὸ ξίφος τῆς δίκης τὸ ἔχον πικρίαν [the sword of justice that has bitterness].
He wounds with a piercing, bitterly sharp sword.
the sword of justice that has bitterness
The Curses raised the sharp cry.
And breathing out a sharp slaughter of blood.
Do you not hear the sharpness of my words?
For beware of the sharp-mouthed griffins.
The tragedians seem to have used only this form, not the Ionic ὀπηδός [attendant], just as they said κυναγός [hunter], not κυνηγός [hunter]: see Lobeck on Phryn. p. 431 and Thes. vol. 5 p. 2079.
